# What You See Is What You Get {.bg-print}

::: incremental
-   **WYSIWYG** word processors show the final layout as you type
-   Examples:
    -   Microsoft Word
    -   LibreOffice
    -   Google Docs
    -   Apple Pages

:::

# $\LaTeX$ {.bg-printers .big-title}

"LaTeX (/ˈlɑːtɛk/ LAH-tek or /ˈleɪtɛk/ LAY-tek, often stylized as $\LaTeX$) is a software system for typesetting documents. LaTeX markup describes the content and layout of the document, as opposed to the formatted text found in WYSIWYG word processors[^1]."

[^1]: <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LaTeX>

# Why use $\LaTeX$? {.bg-printers}

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Strengths**

::: incremental
-   Beautiful mathematics
-   Consistent formatting, automatically
-   Numbering and cross-references that update themselves
-   References and bibliographies managed for you
-   Plain text: works well with version control
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Trade-offs**

::: incremental
-   A learning curve
-   You write *markup*, then compile
-   Fine layout control can be fiddly
-   Not always ideal for heavily visual documents
:::
:::
:::

# How it works {.bg-printers}

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-align: center
flowchart LR
  A[".tex file<br>+ .bib + images"] --> B["LaTeX engine<br>(e.g. pdfLaTeX)"]
  B --> C["PDF"]
  B --> D["Log:<br>warnings and errors"]
```

-   You edit **source**; the engine **compiles** it into a PDF
-   If something is wrong, the **log** tells you where

# Overleaf in 60 seconds {.bg-typer .overleaf-slide}

::: incremental
1.  **New Project** → blank project, or pick a **template**
2.  **Editor** on the left, **PDF preview** on the right
3.  **Recompile** after changes (`Ctrl/Cmd + Enter`)
4.  **Logs and errors** appear under the preview. Fix the first error first
5.  **File tree** (top left): upload images and `.bib` files here
6.  **Menu**: choose the compiler, the main document and the TeX Live version
:::

# Working together in Overleaf {.bg-typer .overleaf-slide}

::: incremental
-   **Share** a project by link or by email, with edit or view-only rights
-   **History** lets you see and restore earlier versions
-   **Comments** can be attached to any piece of text
-   **Track changes** and **Git/GitHub sync** are available on some plans
:::

::: aside
Check which features your account or institution includes.
:::

# The file structure {.bg-typer}

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: incremental
-   Document class
-   Packages
-   Metadata
-   Begin/End document
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
``` latex
\documentclass{article}

\usepackage{amsmath}

\title{My first document}
\author{Your Name}

\begin{document}

\maketitle

\end{document}
```
:::
:::

# `\documentclass{}` {.bg-typer}

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
This command defines the document type. The most frequently used are:

::: incremental
-   `article`
-   `report`
-   `book`
-   `beamer` (slides)
:::

Options go in square brackets, e.g. `\documentclass[12pt,a4paper]{article}`
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
<br>

``` {.latex code-line-numbers="1-1"}
\documentclass{article}

\usepackage{amsmath}

\title{My first document}
\author{Your Name}

\begin{document}

\maketitle

\end{document}
```
:::
:::

# `\usepackage{}` {.bg-typer}

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Packages expand the capabilities of $\LaTeX$. Some examples are:

::: incremental
-   `amsmath`: advanced maths
-   `graphicx`: images
-   `xcolor`: colours
-   `booktabs`: nicer tables
-   `hyperref`: clickable links and references
:::

Packages are loaded in the **preamble**, before `\begin{document}`.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
<br>

``` {.latex code-line-numbers="3"}
\documentclass{article}

\usepackage{amsmath}

\title{My first document}
\author{Your Name}

\begin{document}

\maketitle

\end{document}
```
:::
:::

# Metadata {.bg-typer}

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Defined in the preamble, and printed by `\maketitle` in the main text.

::: incremental
-   `\title{}`
-   `\author{}`
-   `\date{}`: defaults to today; use `\date{}` to hide it
:::

Some classes and templates add more (e.g. `\subtitle{}`), but standard `article` does not have it.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
<br>

``` {.latex code-line-numbers="5-6,10"}
\documentclass{article}

\usepackage{amsmath}

\title{My first document}
\author{Your Name}

\begin{document}

\maketitle

\end{document}
```
:::
:::

# `\begin{document}` / `\end{document}` {.bg-typer}

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Everything between these two lines is the main text and appears in the compiled PDF.

::: incremental
-   Text
-   Equations
-   Figures
-   Tables
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
<br>

``` {.latex code-line-numbers="8,12"}
\documentclass{article}

\usepackage{amsmath}

\title{My first document}
\author{Your Name}

\begin{document}

\maketitle

\end{document}
```
:::
:::

# Sections, paragraphs and text {.bg-typer}

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: incremental
-   `\section{}`, `\subsection{}` create numbered headings
-   `\tableofcontents` builds the contents list. Compile twice to update it
-   A **blank line** starts a new paragraph
-   `\textbf{}` for bold, `\emph{}` for emphasis
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
``` {.latex code-line-numbers="5,7,9,11"}
\documentclass{article}

\begin{document}

\tableofcontents

\section{Introduction}
This is a paragraph. A blank line
starts a new one. Use \textbf{bold}
and \emph{emphasis}.

\subsection{Background}
More text.

\end{document}
```
:::
:::

# Lists {.bg-typer}

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: incremental
-   `itemize` gives bullet points
-   `enumerate` gives numbered items
-   Each entry starts with `\item`
-   Lists can be nested
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
``` latex
\begin{itemize}
  \item First point
  \item Second point
\end{itemize}

\begin{enumerate}
  \item Step one
  \item Step two
\end{enumerate}
```
:::
:::

# Mathematics {.bg-typer}

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: incremental
-   **Inline** expressions go between two `$` signs
-   **Display** equations use the `equation` environment
    -   Numbered automatically
    -   `equation*` (needs `amsmath`) is unnumbered
-   `align` lines up multi-line equations
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
``` {.latex code-line-numbers="6,8-10"}
\documentclass{article}
\usepackage{amsmath}

\begin{document}

Inline math: $E = mc^2$

\begin{equation}
  E = mc^2
\end{equation}

\end{document}
```
:::
:::

# Maths cheat sheet {.bg-typer}

| You want         | You type                        |
|------------------|---------------------------------|
| Fraction         | `\frac{a}{b}`                   |
| Superscript      | `x^2`, `x^{10}`                 |
| Subscript        | `x_i`, `x_{ij}`                 |
| Square root      | `\sqrt{x}`                      |
| Sum              | `\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i`            |
| Greek letter     | `\alpha`, `\beta`, `\Omega`     |

# Cross-referencing {.bg-typer}

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Equations can be referred to from the main text.

::: incremental
-   Two commands do the job:
    -   `\label{}` names the equation
    -   `\ref{}` points to it
-   Put `\label` **inside** the environment
-   Use `~` before `\ref` to avoid a line break
-   Compile **twice** so numbers update
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
``` {.latex code-line-numbers="6,8-11"}
\documentclass{article}
\usepackage{amsmath}

\begin{document}

Energy is given by Eq.~\ref{eq:energy}.

\begin{equation}
  E = mc^2
  \label{eq:energy}
\end{equation}

\end{document}
```
:::
:::

# Figures {.bg-typer}

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: incremental
-   `figure` is a *float*: $\LaTeX$ decides where it lands
    -   `[htbp]` = here, top, bottom, own page
-   `\includegraphics` inserts the image
    -   Dimensions go inside `[ ]`
    -   The filename goes inside `{ }`
    -   Upload the image to your Overleaf project first
-   `\caption{}` first, then `\label{}`
-   Refer to it with `Figure~\ref{fig:myfig1}`
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
``` {.latex code-line-numbers="2,6-11,13"}
\documentclass{article}
\usepackage{graphicx}

\begin{document}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=8cm]{myplot}
  \caption{My plot.}
  \label{fig:myfig1}
\end{figure}

See Figure~\ref{fig:myfig1}.

\end{document}
```
:::
:::

# Tables {.bg-typer}

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: incremental
-   `table` is a float, like `figure`
-   `tabular` draws the table itself
    -   `{lcc}`: one letter per column: left, centre, right
    -   `&` separates cells, `\\` ends a row
-   `booktabs` gives clean rules: `\toprule`, `\midrule`, `\bottomrule`
-   Put `\caption` and `\label` **above** the table (usual convention)
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
``` {.latex code-line-numbers="2,10-17"}
\documentclass{article}
\usepackage{booktabs}

\begin{document}

\begin{table}[htbp]
  \centering
  \caption{Results.}
  \label{tab:results}
  \begin{tabular}{lcc}
    \toprule
    Group & Mean & SD \\
    \midrule
    A & 1.2 & 0.3 \\
    B & 1.8 & 0.4 \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table}

\end{document}
```
:::
:::

# $Bib\TeX$ {.bg-typer}

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: incremental
-   $Bib\TeX$ is a bibliography database file format
-   It is the basis for citations and references in $\LaTeX$
-   Files are saved with the `.bib` extension
-   Each entry has a type, a **key** and `field = {value}` pairs
-   You rarely type these by hand: reference managers, Google Scholar and journal websites can export `.bib`
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
``` bibtex
@article{smith2024,
  author  = {Smith, Jane},
  title   = {An example article},
  journal = {Journal of Examples},
  year    = {2024}
}
```
:::
:::

# References {.bg-typer}

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: incremental
-   `\bibliographystyle{plain}` sets the citation style
    -   Several styles are built in
    -   More can be added with `.bst` files
-   `\bibliography{refs}` prints the references cited and reads `refs.bib`
-   `\cite{}` cites an entry. The text in braces is the key from the `.bib` file
-   After adding citations, recompile (sometimes twice) so they resolve
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
``` {.latex code-line-numbers="6,8-9"}
\documentclass{article}

\begin{document}

As previously seen elsewhere
\cite{smith2024}.

\bibliographystyle{plain}
\bibliography{refs}

\end{document}
```
:::
:::

# $Bib\TeX$ or `biblatex`? {.bg-typer}

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: incremental
-   **$Bib\TeX$** (with `natbib`): long-established. Many journal templates require it
-   **`biblatex`**: more flexible styles and easier customisation
-   Both use the same `.bib` file
-   When using a journal template, **follow its instructions**
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
``` latex
\usepackage[style=authoryear]{biblatex}
\addbibresource{refs.bib}

...

\parencite{smith2024}

\printbibliography
```
:::
:::

# When things go wrong {.bg-typer}

Read the **first** error in the log: later ones are often knock-on effects.

| Message                      | Usual cause                                                     |
|------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------|
| `Undefined control sequence` | Typo in a command, or a missing `\usepackage`                   |
| `Missing $ inserted`         | `_` or `^` (or a maths symbol) used outside maths mode          |
| `File not found`             | Wrong image name or path, or the file was not uploaded          |
| `Runaway argument` / `Missing }` | Unbalanced braces                                           |
| `\begin{x}` ended by `\end{y}` | A missing or mismatched `\end`                                |
| `??` in the PDF              | A `\ref` or `\cite` that has not resolved yet: recompile        |

Special characters need a backslash: `\%`, `\&`, `\$`, `\#`, `\_`, `\{`, `\}`

# Practical session {.bg-typer .overleaf-slide}

::: incremental
1.  Create a **new blank project** and compile "Hello, world"
2.  Add a title, author and date with `\maketitle`
3.  Add two **sections** and a bulleted list
4.  Write the quadratic formula as a **numbered equation** and refer to it in the text
5.  Upload an image and insert it as a **figure** with a caption
6.  Build a small **table** with `booktabs`
7.  Create `refs.bib`, add one entry and **cite** it
:::

**Stretch:** try a journal template, or switch to `biblatex`
